primarily as sources of calories (and we can get calories
from other macronutrients), no specific requirement has
been set for them (see Chapter 1, The Dietary Reference
Intakes [DRIs], page 5).  But health experts agree that we
should obtain most of our calories (about 60 percent) from
carbohydrates.  Our individual requirements depend on
age, sex, size, and activity level.  
In contrast to the other carbohydrates, fiber (a substance
contained in bran, fruits, vegetables, and legumes) is a type
of complex carbohydrate that cannot be readily digested by
our bodies.  Even though it isn’t digested, fiber is essential
to our health. Nutrition professionals recommend 25 to 30
grams of fiber daily.
Simple Sugars
Simple sugars make foods sweet.  They are small molecules
found in many foods and in many forms.  Some simple
sugars occur naturally in foods.  For example, fructose is the
sugar that naturally gives some fruits their sweet flavor.  
Table sugar, the sugar that we spoon onto our cereal
and add to the cookies we bake, also called sucrose, is the
most familiar simple sugar.  A ring-shaped molecule of
sucrose actually consists of a molecule of fructose chemi-
cally linked to a molecule of another simple sugar called
glucose.  Sugars such as fructose and glucose are known as
monosaccharides, because of their single (mono) ring
